We think that it has to be a very clear mandate on what it means, and I think we continue to discuss what sometimes the discussions mean. And for us, it's very clear that we have an impact on the environment, that this impact unfortunately is necessary— we produce food and that is how food is produced— and that that must be part of the awareness. And we don't think that debates about how much food you produce and the percentage and whether you can take it away brings much to the table because that, you know, if you take it one by one it's okay, but if you take— you start doing that with a lot of food then you end up with a big problem in supply. And for us therefore the question cannot be how we eliminate all those fishing impacts because to completely eliminate all impacts of fisheries can only be done by eliminating fisheries itself. And that is eliminating a lot of knowledge, communities and other— and I'm not exaggerating by saying that this is what everybody's advocating, but I think it's an important point to make on the other side. To frame our situation— and I'm sorry about a lot of words there— well, the first thing we'd like to say is that we fishermen are very, very worried about the situation of the ocean and we are very, very involved in its preservation and its future. We have to remind and to say continuously that If there is no healthy ocean, there is no fisheries. If there is no fisheries, there is no fishing industry, and more importantly, there is no fishing people. And that is the biggest commitment we can do. I don't think there is any other sector economically that depends so much on the health of the ocean and its productiveness. So that has to be said. We also, as we said, we are fully aware that our activity has an impact on the environment and that we need to moderate it, curtail it, regulate it, and, you know, follow everything that has been said in the previous panels, and we very much participate in that effort. We also think that it's very important to break some stereotypes and avoid generalisation. Generalisation creates problems, and that is a little bit one of the critics. When we speak about fisheries sometimes, we speak as if all fisheries were the same. As if all bottom trawling is the same, as all RFMOs are the same, and they're certainly not. There are very many differences, many stemming from cultures, from gears, but also from economic development. I've heard yesterday speak about— well, I think it was some NGO that is no longer here on the conference, but we were talking about the heavy chains that you have on the bottom trawl nets That is no longer the case in many, in most developed fisheries because it's very inefficient, it consumes a lot of fuel and it's much better to do efforts like the ones presented by Spain this morning with the semi-pelagic doors and less contact with the bottom. And sometimes I like to say it like that, but if you don't believe us on what we say and you believe we are greedy— I apologize for the language— we are greedy bastards, well, It just makes more money not to trawl 16 tonnes of chain through the bottom. And I really mean this. I think there is a lot of development and that has to be taken into account. And also we have to look on why there isn't that development in some regions because there might be ways to solve that if the proper investment is done there. And that is what I mean with bottom trawling not being the same everywhere. I'm not trying to say some are better than others. But I think some are more able, whether it's economically or technically, than others, and that is something that needs to be addressed. I think also the interpretation of protection targets and commitment is not always the same. When we speak about commitment and protection, sometimes we have the feeling we come from different objectives, and I think this is very complicated for the debate, not only in global level but also our informal level. when we compare different RFMOs or areas without RFMOs, but also inside the fleets themselves. And by fleets I mean fleets of different countries, of different flags. There are different compliances, there are different national rules, and even within national rules there are different actors acting in many different ways. And I think this is a problem as well because if you put everybody on the same bag then those who are actually striving to do better fishing and trying to reduce the commitment, the impacts, well, they need to be rewarded somehow or at least not penalised because otherwise you create frustration and frustration is very big in the fishing industry these days, I have to say. And I think that is quite unanimous. Any fishing nation, and there are many here present, can say that if you talk to the industry they are frustrated in many levels. And it's a difficult situation for us. I think one of the main issues is the lack— we feel we are still not trusted actors on the issue. You know, all fishing goes around the fishing industry, yet the fishing industry very often is pointed at as the problem maker and not the solution maker or part of the solution. I don't like being that victim. I don't do that. I think we need to engage more and we need to tell our story better. I think we are quite quite guilty of sometimes of being a little bit secretive and a little bit maybe introvert, but I think also it's a little bit justified. Very often those who provide more data and are more open are the ones signalled afterwards using that same data that they have produced. And very often other fleets that are more secretive and less transparent are left out, and then when you ask about some campaigners, they say, well, there is no data about them, we cannot— produce any reports. Well, yeah, but that's quite unfair as well. So I think this is very important, setting the future. Also, this creates a lot of doubts on the future of fisheries sometimes, and that is actually one of the main problems for collecting more investment that can lead to better gear and better technology. And also, ironically, I think that putting the future of fisheries in doubt also reduces the investment in fisheries research, and that is a problem. We see that in RFMOs, the member states are having more and more problem in finding fishing scientists, and, you know, at the same time we are giving more and more work to them, and that creates a problem. And then ironically, fisheries— the fishing industry can provide the more supportable solutions because— or the more simple which is gear technology, fishing tactics, vessel design. And one thing that is, I think, very much overlooked is that if the right trust is created— and I'm not talking about not being open with data, but some data is proprietary, and if you look at other industries, that confidentiality of data is very much respected, not so much in fisheries. We have to find a way to do it. Vessels can and should be major producers of data. We are all the time in the middle of the sea, we are collecting fish, but we have a lot of technology in our bridges, we know a lot now about depths, temperatures, and I— in the data— in the era of big data, we should be one of the major suppliers. But also sometimes we are faced with problems supplying the data. There are no proper channels, there are no protocols, and there is even some people who say that that data cannot be used, and we should find a way for that, because we really, really want to contribute there. So that is how we see it, and how we would like to see it is to change a little bit the debate. I think one thing that is very necessary to define is what is an acceptable impact. We are food-producing. I'm not saying it should be A or B, but I think when you set up a lot of objectives on protection, you also have to be aware we are producing food. Yesterday in one— I think it was in the side event— I asked a question to the panelists and I said, if you take the same analysis you're doing on seamounts— and honestly, I am not entering the debate on seamounts. I explained that yesterday and I'm willing to answer a question on that.
Yes.

But if you do it on an agricultural production, you will get very similar results. If you analyse from the perspective that sometimes fisheries is analysed, a cornfield, you will find that there is a heavy reduction of biodiversity, that there is a complete transformation of the local ecosystem and a permanent, probably, transformation. And I'm not saying that justifies anything. What I'm saying is trying to put it in perspective. We saw today from the FAO and the Deep Sea Project that in RFMOs we are trawling 2.3, I think it was the data, percent of the RFMO area. So we need to put that in perspective. When you hear the debate sometimes it looks like we, on the— every morning we wake up with a vessel, we tie a net on the back and we just go around seeing to look if we and find fish. That is not at all how fisheries is. We keep going back and back to the same fishing grounds, which is the best proof that they're still productive. So what is an acceptable impact is something that needs to be decided along with the protection measures. What— the distinction between ongoing activities and future activities is very important. It's not the same to trawl in an area that has been trawled for over 60 or 80 years in a very contained area than to open new fisheries. And that is a distinction that we in the industry are very clear about and I think that is very important. That is why we talk so much about the footprint. Past impacts, yes, I don't disagree that 80 years ago maybe we should have not trolled in certain areas. Knowledge was what it was, but the fact is that happened and that area has been changed, it's not a trolling area. Maybe it's best to keep it, therefore, there and do it in a manner that is compatible with conservation and preservation of the ecosystem. And that's what I mean with respecting existing fishing areas as food production areas. And then finally, very clearly on the debate, we in the fishing industry, we are completely committed to the conservation of the ocean, but for us that does not mean no activity at all. Or no area. We know that there will be areas that will be heavily impacted and others not. The aspiration of 30 by 30 for us seems a little bit void because on the worst estimation that I've read, 40% of the world's seas have been fished, which is way, way overestimated, but let's accept that data for a moment. That means we can protect 60% of the sea. So when we talk about percentages, Let's, you know, look where we preserve and all that. And there is way too much focus on the footprint, and we do that because that's where the science takes place, but we are not looking enough outside of the footprint and seeing what is out there and, you know, really what can be— it's hard to say, but sacrificed in the sense of continuing to produce food. This is very important. I think it has to be clear And I don't think the objective of the resolutions was to fully protect the sea and completely leave it untouched, and certainly not for other activities, and I don't think it's the case for fisheries either. So we need science, we need more sources of science, integrate knowledge, we need more mapping of the oceans, not just the fishing operates, we need other factors than fishing to be put on the scale. Very often when we talk about RFMOs we know that there are exogenous reasons to fisheries that are affecting the fish stocks or even the conservation of the bottom, but there's nothing we can do. All we can do is regulate fisheries when we know the problem is maybe oil production or mining, and that makes no sense. And I think Bibi and Jay produce— brings a very good maybe factor into this debate. We also need to ask other sectors to provide information like we do. Fisheries produces all the information, VMS data, etc. You might not like where we give it, but it's given. We give it to the flag states, they have it. We give every single trawl of production that we have. There are other sectors who are blasting the sea to look at the shape of the bottom of the sea and then we don't get the results of that, not even the shape of the sea. And that is tremendously important because as we all know, the shape of the sea, of the ocean, of the ocean floor can be actually a VME protector indicator, so we need that information and that is not there. And this is clearly something that needs to be more integrated, and we think that VB&J provides a very interesting idea for this. And again, I already spoke about the— and I come to my last slide. So the other thing that we'd like to see is to develop more proper metrics of sustainability with net gains and losses for each decision. If you reduce production of food in one area, you might be creating a need for more production in another area. We hear a lot about agriculture, but also, let's be honest, agriculture brings a lot of sediment and fertilizers and others to the sea, so we have to be very open when we look at the conservation of the sea. And again, we know fisheries is easy to look at and it's very obvious, but there are many other activity sectors, some of them not evident, that have a tremendous impact on the ocean, on the health of the ocean. We have to look about the MPAs and its objectives, and they have to be clear beyond the ending of fishing activities, which is sometimes what we hear, but also to define them in a pragmatic and not absolute manner. I'm talking about OCMs and to even look at, you know, when we talk about an RFMO, it's actually a very managed area and it's very protected. The areas are being continuously closed and regulated for protection of bottom sea— of the bottom of the ocean and other objectives, and that certainly has to count for something because it's much better than other areas which have no look at all. Finally, We also want to talk about the strengthening of governance, recognize difficulties of enforcement and role of non-party flag states as well as objecting parties. What I mean with this is what we spoke about RFMOs, we have to be very clear one thing: not always being in RFMO, even if there is a binding decision, means every party will follow it. You can always object to it and do it on the side, and that is something that has to be taken account. If you take it to the extreme in BBNJ, there are 92— 96 countries that have signed, but that means there is 100 who haven't signed, and those will be not obligated at all under any circumstance to the treaty, and, you know, when you take the treaty to the RFMOs, again, they will be not obligated. You might be, without intention, created— and I use this word very carefully— winners, in the sense that if you close areas for production under BBNJ and you're bound to it, but the other party is not, then they might conduct the fisheries, no problem, and the surprise is that there is no problem attached. You can still sell that fish in the same markets that have decided themselves to stop fishing in an area. And this happens. This happens more than you think. And I come from the European Union, which is the biggest market in the world for seafood, and we are very, very good at not putting any problem for the fish coming in. But doing it for the one we produce ourselves, and that is a major flaw in governance. Actually, when we try to do that inside of the EU, we are told that that goes against the WTO, which I think is very odd that we— you know, if you don't enforce something that has been agreed internationally, you cannot use it to curtail trade and put it outside. So I'm not a particular fan, for obvious reasons, of CITES and IUCN. We had had very bad examples fisheries, but I think if it's well used they could be potentially very good. It has not been the case, I want to be on the record saying that. Look-alike species and so on are not the way to do. What I'm saying is to really look into this. And finally, again, stress very importantly the BB&J opportunity it brings. I think it's the right time to bring everything under not one umbrella, because the treaty is what it is, but the opportunities that Charlotte very well pointed out before, is you can bring coherence into the debate, you can bring the RFMOs to be equivalent to the impact assessments, you can create, well, references for the RFMOs to all become at the same level. There is a myriad of things that can be done. Member states will also have to do some IAAs inside their own waters if they have any affectation on the international waters. So It is a very good way to maybe not have 35 fora where we speak about the same thing, but actually bring everything together. Some— a lot of us were in this room 2 months ago talking about the fish stocks agreement in BB&J, and the discussion is very similar, yet the legal instruments are very different. So this is an opportunity, and you will find that the fishing industry will be present at the debate. willing to collaborate and willing to be part of the solution, but we also want to be recognized as an actor that wants to be sustainable and wants more than anybody probably to preserve the sea because preserving the sea is preserving its own identity and existence. This will be our only red line. And enjoy eating food. You will be happier. This is a proven fact. Thank you.

during this workshop. But speaking of the workshop in general, dear delegates, we now have our last panelist for the workshop, and the person who gets the honor is Matthew Gianni, co-founder of the Deep Sea Conservation Coalition, the DSCC. Okay, thank you, Madam Moderator. I'll wait till the presentation comes up on the screen, but just to introduce the Deep Sea Conservation Coalition, my first 2 slides. It is a coalition of over 140 organizations worldwide looking to protect deep-sea ecosystems from multiple anthropogenic impacts or threats. And we're working on a range of issues, including but not limited to the question of bottom fisheries on the high seas. Just a bit of history with the seamounts— I'm sorry, the UNGA resolutions, which I was involved in from the very beginning through the United Nations informal consultative process, as were some of the other people in the room here. I'm looking at Peter Oster, for example. In 2022— I'm sorry, 2002, the General Assembly first called for urgent consideration of the risks to the biodiversity of seamounts and other underwater features. And that's Resolution, the oceans— the omnibus resolution, 57-141. Many countries, scientists, the DSCC, and other NGOs called for a moratorium on bottom trawling on the high seas to protect seamounts unless or until they could be managed consistent with international law. And in 2004, the first substantive call for action, UNGA Resolution 5925. Yes. 5 was adopted, which included language in paragraph 67, I believe it was, including consideration of an interim prohibition on bottom trawling on seamounts impacting VMEs. And as you all know, an agreement was reached 20 years ago in Resolution 2006/61.05 and reinforced in 2009/6472, grounded in key Fish stocks agreements and provisions, or obligations I should say, as follows. So states individually and through RFMOs commit to manage bottom fisheries in ABNJ to prevent significant adverse impacts on VMEs through a conducting prior impact assessments before bottom fishing is permitted, and that's consistent with Article or derives from draws from Article 5D of the Fish Stocks Agreement. Establish Precautionary area closures to protect VMEs where VMEs are known or likely to occur unless bottom fishing can be managed to prevent significant adverse impacts, and that draws on the Fish Stocks Agreement Articles 5G, 6.1, 6.2, 6.3D. Ensuring sustainable catch, rebuilding depleted stocks, and minimizing bycatch and/or impacts of fishing on other deep-sea species, in particular vulnerable or threatened endangered species is consistent with Article 5F and 5H, protecting biodiversity in the marine environment. And finally, paragraph 120 of General Assembly Resolution 6472 adopted in 2009 said adopt and implement these measures or else not authorize bottom fisheries to proceed. And this was actually a precursor to the negotiation of the the BBNJ agreement, particularly with their key elements on environmental impact assessments and area-based management measures, as well as precautionary approach and reverse burden of proof, something that Charlotte touched on. And I would add that the presentation of Duolos at the informal consultation of states parties to the UN Fish Stocks Agreement that took place here in May details the biodiversity conservation provisions quite well in the fish stocks agreement as complementary to and in some cases more stronger than what's in the BBNJ agreement. And these I just put out the more or less the text of these Articles 5D, 5G, 6 through , et cetera, that I've just made reference to in the previous slide. I'll skip this one for the moment. So bottom trawling on seamounts is incompatible in our view with growing high-level international political commitments and the BBNJ agreement. And you have commitments, for example, to halt and reverse biodiversity loss. There are commitments that have been adopted at high levels to protect and restore the health, productivity, and resilience of ocean ecosystems. And these are found in instruments such as the Future We Want, the outcome document from the Rio+20 conference, the Leaders' Pledge to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030, which was initiated by the UN Secretary-General, I believe, signed by 99 heads of state. The 2030 Sustainable Development Goals, in particular SDG 14 Target 2, which calls— commits states to build the resilience and the restoration of marine ecosystems, and the UN Decade of Ecosystem Restoration. And the BBNJ agreement now incorporates some of these into international law. Through its Article 7, and again Charlotte mentioned some of these, but the BBNJ Agreement should— involves implementing principles and approaches including an approach that builds ecosystem resilience including to adverse impacts of climate change and also maintains and restores ecosystem integrity. The UNGA resolutions as I mentioned earlier and the Fish Stocks Agreement and the BBNJ Agreement are intertwined. Again, focused on impact assessments, ABNTs, VME protection, etc. And on the question of science, we've heard much science over the last few days— or the last 2 days, actually. It feels like more than that. But just a few quotes from the UN's First World Ocean Assessment and its chapter on biological communities on seamounts and other submarine features. And quote, the vast majority of deepwater fisheries have been carried out unsustainably. Second bullet point, quick. Quote, fishing and in particular deepwater trawling has caused severe widespread long-term destruction of these, in reference to seamount environments globally. Quote, third bullet point, the widespread destruction of deepwater benthic communities due to trawling has presumably reduced their ecological and evolutionary resilience. Resilience as a result of reduced reproductive potential and loss of genetic diversity and ecological connectivity. And then a fourth that I'm simply summarizing, which is the final paragraph in that chapter of the World Ocean Assessment, that without understanding connectivity amongst species and ecosystems, VMEs, it is not possible to know what and how much is being protected through bottom fisheries area closures. And the World Ocean Assessment II in 2021 concluded in its summary in Chapter 7L entitled Seamounts and Pinnacles, fishing, especially bottom trawling, constitutes the greatest current threat to seamount ecosystems. And I believe IUCN may have— Simi Payne from IUCN may have mentioned that as well. And all of this kind of confirms or is reflected in the type of science and now on a more updated basis that we've heard from Amy Bakko-Taylor and Savannah Goode and some of the other scientists that have made presentations both here on the panels and in the side event on Monday. The UN Secretary-General's report, kind of updating what's been happening since 2022, and contains a number of very useful— quite a lot of very useful information. I'm just excerpting a few of the points in the report, but for example, connectivity among VME indicator species, particularly for population on seamounts, is incredibly complex. Low genetic diversity can make these species less resilient to disturbance, e.g., climate change, and human impacts, i.e., some of the other impacts that Yvonne was talking about. Fish biodiversity also increases between depths of 400 to 1,000 meters. And this— I'll come back to this, but there are relatively large numbers of species, not necessarily amounts, but a variety of species, more so it seems than in shallow-water trawl fisheries that are caught in these depths, which are generally the depths, 400 to 1,000 meters, that the deep-water trawling takes place. The report refers to— reports note that bottom trawling is linked to Rapid declines in both target and non-target species, and then it makes reference to some new information that's emerged since 2022 from New Zealand, from from the North and South Pacific. There is information from other areas as well, but New Zealand and Australia have reported that 231 species and 281 genera of VME indicator taxa, as well as unnamed species, have been observed as bycatch in the high seas. Bottom trawl fisheries, I should say, in the— well, bottom fisheries, I assume it's trawl fisheries predominantly— in the Southwest Pacific and Tasman Sea. And that NPFC has identified 128 species of fish caught in bottom fishery surveys on the Emperor Seamount chain on the high seas of the North Pacific, of which a handful are commercially targeted species of fish. And I would simply note that those surveys have been done by commercial bottom trawlers. And it's to their credits, to the credit of New Zealand and Japan and other countries that have established 100% observer coverage on bottom trawl fisheries since the conclusion or since the adoption of Resolution 61/105. But the information is indicating that there— it's a major challenge to, for example, to attempt an impact assessment On the— on whether or not bottom fisheries, and in particular bottom trawl fisheries, can be managed to prevent significant adverse impacts on all of the species associated with and dependent upon VMEs. These are communities of species. It's not just VME indicator species. And I'll come back to this. I think this has been mentioned before in Melanie Virtue's presentation, but also of course Simmie Payne's presentation from yesterday. But other IFBs, instruments, frameworks, and bodies, have called for action to protect seamounts. CMS COP16 prioritized the protection of seamount ecosystems from multiple threats, including overfishing and destructive fish practice. And as Eduardo Svoglia from Brazil mentioned this morning, this was adopted in March of this year at the CMS COP16 in Brazil. The IUCN World Conservation Congress Resolution 032 called for activating a transition away from bottom trawling on seamounts at the UN General Assembly in 2000— by— well, in 2006. This was the World Conservation Congress in 2005. And this is not new. The CBD Decision 75 in 2004 actually led to the first substantive General Assembly call for action to protect— prevent destructive fishing practices consequences on VMEs including seamounts, cold-water corals, and hydrothermal vents in the resolution adopted in 2004, Resolution 5925. The CBD decision language was incorporated almost verbatim into the General Assembly resolution adopted later that year. So coming back to where the UNGA review stands today. It will be largely based on the resolution— the language in the resolution adopted at the conclusion of the last bottom fisheries review in 2022. That was Resolution 77118. That language on bottom fisheries has been carried through to the most recent fisheries resolution, 8109, adopted in 2025. And that will form the basis of the review by the UN General Assembly and whether any further actions are required. And just to go through a bit of that language, this is the newer stuff more or less, but paragraph 211 of 77/118 recognizes— the General Assembly recognizes the need for further progress with regard to obtaining more biological information on the species that comprise vulnerable marine ecosystems, including their associated and dependent species, the assessment of significant adverse impacts on vulnerable marine ecosystems, and protecting biodiversity— protecting and conserving biodiversity including beyond vulnerable marine ecosystems. And I'm taking this language verbatim from the resolutions. 2012, paragraph 2012 states, identify and overcome barriers to the implementation of the relevant paragraphs of General Assembly resolutions, the previous paragraphs that are the subject of this workshop here today and yesterday, this week, and 2013 to ensure that the precautionary approach is applied, including in the utilization of impact assessments to inform management decisions and consideration of significant adverse impacts on vulnerable marine ecosystems, including their associated and dependent species. So tall orders coming from the UNGA, but the associated and dependent species is actually language in Article 5D of the Fish Stocks Agreement that is in the— which addresses the obligation to assess the impacts on target stocks, non-target species, and associated dependent species with the target stocks in the management of fisheries for straddling fish stocks and highly migratory fish stocks, including on the high seas. So just to cut this short, the recommendation from our side is that the United Nations General Assembly, given all the information we now know coming from the scientific communities, from research done from the UN, incorporated into the UN's World Ocean Assessments, the UN Secretary-General's report, that the General Assembly should call for a phase-out of bottom trawling on seamounts as part of the UNGA review this year. The science clearly shows it is not possible to manage bottom trawling on seamounts to prevent SAIs on VMEs, including their many associated and dependent species and their connectivity, about which little scientific information has been obtained. And I'm talking about the hundreds of bycatch species, whether benthic species associated with vulnerable marine ecosystems or the fish, sharks, rays, and other chondrichthyan species that are demersal and inhabiting seamount ecosystems. You know, on or near the bottom. And it would be possible to conduct proper impact assessments to determine whether these fisheries could be managed until that scientific information is obtained. And I think it echoes something that Norway said. It could take decades to do that. There are many species, little scientific information is known, but many of which are recognized as probably or vulnerable because of the depths in which they inhabit, the slow-growing nature and late age of maturity and low fecundity, for example, characteristic of deep-sea species as compared to shallow-water species. And nor can they be managed to build ecosystem resilience or restore ecosystem integrity as called for in numerous political commitments and the obligations under the Fish Stocks Agreement and now the BBNJ Agreement Article 7. To the contrary, they can continue to degrade seamount ecosystems and their resilience. And so the best way to overcome barriers to the implementation of the relevant paragraphs of the UN General Assembly, which is in paragraph 2012 of the 2022 GA resolution, and to bridge this major gap in implementation would be to implement paragraph 120 of the resolution 6472 to not authorize bottom trawl fishing on seamounts to proceed. And this is really a question of international law and should apply to all fishing on the high seas on seamounts and not just some or many or most. There should be no exceptions as a matter of rule if, in fact, these obligations are to be applied to fisheries overall in terms of ecosystem protection in the sustainability of deep sea stocks. So with that, let me conclude and say thank you.

Thank you, Madam Chair. I'm reading this statement on behalf of Greenpeace, Oceans North, NRDC, DSEC, DOCI, and Pew. This review is a crucial milestone since the adoption of UNGA Resolution 61/105 20 years ago. There has been progress compared to the situation 2 decades ago. However, Since the last review in 2022, we have been far too slow to match the urgency of biodiversity loss and degradation these ecosystems are facing. Significant adverse impacts on vulnerable marine ecosystems continue, and implementation measures remain insufficient to deliver the commitments states have already made. The discussions over the past 2 days have demonstrated that the issue is no longer solely due to a lack of scientific knowledge. Science continues to show that VMEs are unprotected and at risk of SAIs in many high-seas areas. Our presentations showed cases where strong scientific evidence was provided of presence and damage to VMEs and was not followed by the adoption by RFMO parties of the measures required to protect these ecosystems. The science presented in segment 1 of this workshop as well as the debate yesterday and today, has provided clear evidence on the need to expand protection of VMEs and globally phase out bottom trawling over seamounts and similar features. There are other important aspects of the sustainability of deep-sea fisheries where clearly progress by States and RFMOs to implement their responsibilities under UNGA resolutions and UNCLOS more generally has been limited. Like the sustainability of deep-sea populations or the impacts on associated and dependent species, and addressing the impacts of climate change. Given their life history traits, deep-sea species are extremely vulnerable to fishing pressure. Much progress is needed on that front too, as the FAO recognized in its presentation yesterday.
